issues.item: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, a trigger based on being in a similar natural environment is hard to reconcile unless the robbery specifically occurred in wilderness or outdoors; nothing else in the profile supports that context, making this trigger clinically incongruent with the rest of the presentation.

Helicopter/aircraft sounds are not a plausible trauma-linked trigger for a mugging/robbery in the absence of any supporting memory or threat content suggesting emergency-response, combat, or disaster context. This appears disconnected from the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to link clinically unless the robbery specifically involved aircraft or a major police response; this trigger is not supported by the other selected items and feels trauma-incongruent.

Alcohol smell could occur if the perpetrator had been drinking, but that link is not reflected anywhere else in the profile, so as selected it appears weakly grounded in the trauma narrative compared with the other more plausible interpersonal-danger cues.

These appraisals fit poorly with the stated trauma type and with the other selected items.

issues.explanation: Burnt smell is a highly specific trigger that suggests fire, smoke, or explosion exposure. In a robbery/mugging profile it lacks support from the threat and appraisal items and does not connect plausibly to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery in a 67-year-old male, 'body shame' is hard to reconcile unless there was prominent sexual assault, disfigurement, or injury-focused trauma content, which is not reflected elsewhere in threat, memory, or strategies. It reads as a qualitatively different appraisal from the rest of the profile.

issues.explanation: 'Burnt smell' is not a plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery unless there was specific fire/smoke/burning content in the trauma, which is not supported by the other selected items. It appears disconnected from the stated trauma type and from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. The remaining items are broadly coherent with robbery trauma and with the active formulation path Negative Appraisals → Threat and Threat → Triggers.

vignette:
Frank Delaney, a 67-year-old hotel manager, described the robbery as the moment his sense of himself and of other people changed in a way that had never fully settled. One evening, after closing the hotel's bar and front desk, he walked to his car carrying receipts and the day's deposit. In the parking lot a man came up from behind, close enough that Frank caught the sharp smell of alcohol on his breath before he saw the knife. The mugger demanded his wallet and keys, and when Frank hesitated, the man shouted so loudly that the sound seemed to split the night open. Frank remembered the shove, the humiliation of being searched and emptied out under the glow of the lot lights, and the feeling that he looked weak and foolish while other people inside the hotel carried on unaware. Since then, he had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the world was dangerous, and that what happened to him had left him permanently humiliated.

Those beliefs tightened the way he moved through ordinary life. Frank said he was superalert now, especially in places where he could not instantly assess who was near him. At work he found himself scanning the lobby, the bar entrance, the parking lot cameras, and the faces of guests who seemed even slightly suspicious. A man lingering too long near the front desk, someone pacing by the elevators, or a guest reeking of alcohol could make his chest tense before anything was said. Loud noises did the same: a dropped tray in the restaurant, a slammed service door, a sudden burst of laughter in the hallway could send a jolt through him. He had become convinced that staying watchful was the only reason he remained safe, and that if he let his guard down, someone would take advantage of him the way the mugger had.

That constant watchfulness had made the world feel full of warning signs, and Frank now caught danger in moments other people ignored. A stranger standing too still near the entrance, a late-night guest who kept glancing around, the smell of alcohol drifting up from a patio group, or even a sudden shout from the loading dock could all make him flinch and tense before he had time to think. He also startled when someone touched him unexpectedly. His wife might brush his arm in the kitchen or a housekeeper might tap his shoulder in the corridor, and he would react with alarm, heart racing, as if he had been grabbed from behind again. Even at home, where he had once felt settled, he remained on guard, checking the locks twice and listening for noises in the dark hallway before he could relax enough to sit down.

Over the months, Frank began avoiding the situations that made him feel exposed. He started leaving the hotel earlier in the evening, asking other staff to handle the parking lot when possible, and staying close to the desk instead of moving through the building. He took different routes home to avoid bars and blocks where he might smell alcohol or encounter groups of people who looked suspicious. At home he kept the porch light on and was uneasy if the house was too quiet or if a sudden sound came from the street. The changes embarrassed him because he had always seen himself as capable and composed. His wife noticed that he was no longer as willing to go out to dinner, and at work he was shorter with staff when they startled him or when the lobby grew noisy. What began as caution gradually narrowed his world, and the narrowing itself seemed to confirm how dangerous everything had become.

By the time he sought help, Frank was exhausted from feeling as though he had to monitor every person, sound, and smell around him. He said he finally came in after nearly snapping at a guest who came up behind him at the front desk, and then nearly jumping out of his skin when his wife touched his shoulder that same night. What frightened him most was that he no longer trusted his own judgment to tell the difference between ordinary life and danger, and what he hoped for was some way to feel safe again without having to stay braced for an attack every hour of the day.
